title: Beau on the conditions for securitisation to release lending capacity
summary: Denis Beau supports the European Commission’s proposed revision of securitisation rules because he thinks well-designed transactions can expand lending capacity and connect bank balance sheets to capital-market investors. His case turns on which constraint a transaction relieves. Selling or pledging securities can improve funding. Transferring risk in a form recognised by supervisors can change the capital a bank must maintain. Neither operation by itself establishes that a bank will originate an additional loan. Speaking for the Banque de France and the ACPR at the 9 January seminar, Beau therefore ties his support to a package of prudential calibration, operational changes and credible information on the underlying borrowers.

The clearest quantitative evidence concerns refinancing. ABS accounted for close to 30% of marketable securities actually mobilised as Eurosystem collateral, against less than 5% of the eligible universe (p. 1). The first figure describes securities pledged, the second the broader set eligible for use. Their difference signals heavy use of ABS by institutions accessing refinancing. It supplies little evidence about how readily an investor could sell the same security in the secondary market. Beau expected broader ABS eligibility from November 2026 as credit acceptance thresholds were brought into line with other monetary policy asset classes. The prospective change could expand the collateral available to banks. Its practical value would still depend on valuation, haircuts and confidence in the quality of loan-level information.

For the real economy, securitisation converts a pool of assets that would otherwise be difficult to trade into claims that investors can buy. An originator may diversify its sources of funds, manage its exposure and potentially create room for new SME or household lending. Investors gain access to additional investment-grade securities. Beau presents productive investment as a possible use of that capacity. The speech gives neither the volume of incremental credit nor the share expected to reach green or digital projects. The distinction matters because financing existing assets, transferring their risk and funding new capital expenditure are three economically different outcomes (pp. 1–2).

This issue is especially important for green ABS. Beau discusses mortgages on energy-efficient homes and loans on low-emission vehicles. He favours a European Green Bond designation linked to the underlying claims, backed by common loan-level indicators and reporting templates. For property, he would combine energy performance certificates with measures of physical climate risk. One helps assess energy efficiency, while the other speaks to the vulnerability of the collateral itself. Comparable disclosures would let an investor test the environmental claim and assess the credit exposure. A label on the issued security alone cannot establish that a building has become more efficient or less exposed to a physical hazard.

The French authorities see the European market as subdued despite earlier post-crisis initiatives. Beau endorses the direction of the Commission package while recording disagreement over its calibration. Some supervisors, including the ECB and EIOPA identified in note 2, worried about additional risk-taking. Some market participants wanted larger reductions in capital requirements or more operational relief. He proposes clearer disclosure and due-diligence procedures for public and private transactions, and capital charges more closely aligned with the risk of higher-quality structures. Retention, investor information and incentives to maintain underwriting quality remain integral to the proposal. The objective is to lower fixed compliance costs without creating room for the party originating the loan to pass poorly understood risk to another balance sheet (pp. 2–3).

A more immediate operational test concerns the recognition of significant risk transfer. Beau expected a supervisory fast track in the first half of 2026. A standard process could give issuers more predictable timetables, help supervisors allocate staff and free specialist attention for unusual structures. It is a timing and recognition issue distinct from the broader collateral eligibility change expected later in the year. At the speech date neither timetable provided a realised estimate of issuance, investor demand, lending or spreads. For an investor assessing European bank funding, the speech identifies prospective catalysts and the conditions for transmission, while leaving the size and incidence of the benefits open.

questions.question: Which transactions would actually expand the supply of new loans?
questions.detail: The speech explains both a funding channel and a capital-relief channel. Distinguishing them would change a judgement about bank credit growth or profitability. Compare approvals of significant risk transfer, resulting changes in capital requirements and new SME or household originations by participating banks. Supervisory disclosures, issuer transaction documents and subsequent lending reports could establish whether balance-sheet capacity translated into additional lending.

questions.question: How valuable would broader collateral eligibility be to the marginal issuer?
questions.detail: The 30% mobilisation share reveals intensive use of existing ABS but does not measure the funding cost of newly eligible tranches. The relevant comparison is the cost of alternative funding against proceeds after central bank haircuts and transaction expenses. Consult the final Eurosystem eligibility and valuation rules and compare eligible and ineligible instruments of similar underlying quality.

questions.question: Can an investor validate the credit and environmental characteristics of a green pool?
questions.detail: Beau proposes underlying-asset indicators and identifies energy efficiency and physical risk as distinct dimensions. He supplies no distribution of either across outstanding pools. Review an issuer’s loan-level template, certificate coverage, location-specific hazards and treatment of missing data. That evidence would affect whether a pricing difference for a labelled tranche is justified by better information, different credit risk or investor demand.
